content: The availability of resources, including human, financial, and physical assets, is essential to support evaluation activities. When planning an evaluation, it is critical to consider not only the starting point but also the time required to conduct the evaluation and the time needed to demonstrate measurable results. Additionally, the resources available—such as funding, personnel, and necessary equipment or supplies—must be quantified to ensure feasibility. While it is generally recommended that 10% of the total project budget be allocated to evaluation activities, this allocation may not always be practical or sufficient in real-world scenarios. An illustrative format for a monitoring and evaluation (M&E) implementation plan includes defining activities, sub-activities (with responsible staff), timelines (e.g., Gantt charts or due dates), and associated costs (with funding sources). For example, one objective might be to monitor antenatal care service coverage and pregnancy outcomes. The level of detail in the implementation plan should be tailored to meet stakeholders' needs and facilitate effective monitoring of activities as they are executed and completed. Developing an M&E implementation plan allows for proactive planning of data collection needs, enabling prospective data collection when necessary. Retrospective data collection, on the other hand, may introduce biases that compromise the validity of the information. Therefore, careful planning is essential to ensure the reliability of the evaluation. Positive results from M&E of digital health interventions are critical for scaling up these interventions, as they can secure buy-in from stakeholders such as donors and government entities. To achieve this, M&E objectives must align with the overall project goals and stakeholder expectations. Understanding the relationship between project goals, activities, and anticipated outcomes is necessary for selecting an appropriate study design and meaningful success indicators. A well-designed M&E framework begins with addressing fundamental questions: What is the goal of the M&E efforts? How will the process be organized to achieve these goals? How will the achievement of these goals be measured? This process involves articulating the anticipated benefits of the digital health intervention, referred to as claims, to align M&E efforts with stakeholder expectations and drive adoption and scale-up of the intervention. At the core of every digital health system or intervention is a value proposition—a statement that outlines the benefits to end-users, often with an implicit comparison to non-digital or alternative digital solutions. A strong value proposition can drive the successful adoption and sustainability of digital health systems by effectively communicating their value to end-users. For instance, the CommCare platform emphasizes its ability to build mobile apps in days, not months, highlighting its speed and ease of customization. Value propositions describe how the digital health system meets end-user needs, why it is innovative, and why it is superior to the current standard of care. These propositions are foundational to developing a business model that outlines the project's goals and plans for scaling up and achieving sustainability. Claims about the intervention are based on assumptions about end-user needs and serve as the basis for determining M&E objectives and defining evidence needs for stakeholders. Using a claims-based approach to inform M&E objectives offers several advantages. First, articulating claims early ensures alignment with stakeholder expectations, generating evidence for the most valuable components of the intervention. This alignment can encourage stakeholder investment or adoption of the product. Second, identifying key processes and outcomes to monitor or evaluate can streamline M&E efforts, reducing costs by focusing on critical evidence needed for scale-up. Finally, claims guide the selection of indicators to measure key processes and outcomes effectively. All claims must eventually be translated into measurable M&E objectives. For example, a claim might state that proactive SMS vaccination reminders to mothers improve measles vaccine coverage in their children. The corresponding evaluation objective would be to measure changes in measles vaccine coverage among children whose mothers receive SMS reminders compared to those who do not. A hypothesis might predict a 15% improvement in vaccine coverage due to SMS reminders after one year of implementation. The indicator would then measure the percentage of children receiving measles vaccinations through routine immunization services in the preceding year. When evaluating digital health interventions, it is important to determine whether the system optimizes the delivery of an existing validated health intervention or constitutes a novel intervention with unknown effectiveness. For established interventions, evaluation efforts should focus on outcome measures (e.g., changes in health status or disease prevalence) and process measures (e.g., numbers of trained personnel). For novel interventions, validation of the approach and evaluation of health impact are necessary before claims can be formulated. Linking claims to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is also essential, as health systems and stakeholders increasingly seek innovative approaches to achieve universal health coverage (UHC) objectives. Digital health strategies can address various determinants of UHC, such as accountability, supply chain management, human resource availability, healthcare facility access, demand generation, continuous coverage, quality of care, and financial coverage. For example, digital health interventions might facilitate electronic birth registration, reduce stock-outs of essential drugs, increase the availability of trained providers, or improve adherence to clinical protocols. Stakeholders, defined as individuals or organizations with a vested interest in the digital health system or intervention, play a critical role in shaping and supporting M&E efforts. Mapping stakeholders and understanding their expectations are key steps in ensuring the success and sustainability of digital health interventions.
